title: AXIS Capital grows premiums 11% but acquisition costs rise
full_text:
AXIS Capital has reported its 11th consecutive profitable reinsurance quarter and a 13% rise in insurance gross premiums written, but the cost of that growth is becoming harder to ignore: the acquisition cost ratio widened by 2.8 points to 22.5% in the third quarter of 2026, the biggest contributor to a combined ratio that deteriorated from 89.4% to 94.0% year-on-year.
Net income available to common shareholders fell 32% to US$202 million from US$294 million in Q3 2025, and underwriting income dropped 29% to US$134 million. The year-on-year comparisons are unfavourable partly because Q3 2025 was an unusually strong quarter for AXIS, one that saw underwriting income rise 55% to US$153 million and a combined ratio of 85.9%. Even so, the acquisition cost increase is tied to deliberate strategic choices around ACS rather than transient factors, and it has been building across consecutive quarters.
The acquisition cost ratio increase is directly tied to AXIS Capacity Solutions (ACS), a multi-line portfolio unit the Bermuda-headquartered group launched in 2025. ACS is designed to structure and distribute capacity across open brokerage and delegated business, drawing on third-party capital to grow gross lines while limiting AXIS’s own net exposure. The announcement confirms that new property and professional lines business via ACS, along with a higher mix of short-tail lines including marine war, carries structurally higher acquisition costs than the rest of the portfolio.
ACS generated US$449 million in year-to-date gross premiums written growth through Q3 2026, according to AXIS’s investor presentation published alongside the results. The unit gives AXIS a capital-light revenue stream and the ability to grow gross lines on premium-adequate business without fully loading the balance sheet. The trade-off, visible in the Q3 numbers, is that this business model is inherently distribution-intensive: higher commissions to distribution partners flow straight into the acquisition cost line.
The insurance division remained the group’s engine, producing US$1.9 billion in gross premiums written in Q3, a 13% increase, with growth across marine and aviation lines, accident and health, and property and professional lines through ACS. The combined ratio widened to 92.0% from 85.9% a year earlier, driven by higher loss costs and the acquisition cost increase. The current accident year combined ratio, excluding catastrophe and weather-related losses, came in at 87.2%.
Pre-tax catastrophe and weather-related losses of US$75 million, US$44 million of which arose from the Middle East conflict and the Russia-Ukraine war, fell entirely in the insurance segment. Reinsurance reported zero catastrophe losses for the quarter.
That is partly a consequence of how AXIS Re has been repositioned. In Q3 2026, reinsurance gross premiums written rose 4% to US$449 million, primarily driven by higher premiums in agriculture lines, but non-renewals and reduced line sizes in liability lines pulled year-to-date reinsurance gross premiums down 7%. Increased cession rates in liability and motor lines drove net reinsurance premiums written 5% lower even as gross premiums rose 4%. AXIS Re is shrinking its casualty net retention while growing selectively in agriculture and credit lines.
The reinsurance segment’s 11th consecutive profitable quarter came with a 92.4% combined ratio, broadly stable year-on-year. The streak reflects the deliberate de-risking of the book, with short-tail lines representing more than 60% of reinsurance premiums written, according to management commentary from earlier in 2026.
Net investment income rose 14% to US$211 million, as higher yields on a larger fixed maturity portfolio offset the drag from lower cash balances, an effect the company has attributed in previous quarters to the loss portfolio transfer with Enstar completed in April 2025. The market yield on AXIS’s fixed maturities portfolio stood at 5.8% at September 30, against a book yield of 4.9%, meaning future reinvestment should remain accretive.
The group returned US$141 million to common shareholders in the quarter, including US$109 million in buybacks and US$32 million in dividends. Book value per diluted share, excluding accumulated other comprehensive income, rose 2.7% in the quarter to US$84.33, and is up 14.4% over the past twelve months.
Vince Tizzio, president and chief executive of AXIS Capital, said the company was “well-positioned” heading into the remainder of 2026 and 2027, pointing to the “strength of our balance sheet” as providing flexibility for continued investment in products, platforms and talent.
